Here is a refined modern-English rendering of this poem — Chaucer's *"Truth" (Balade de Bon Conseyl)* — preserving its meaning, imagery, and rhyme-royal structure while elevating the diction into more eloquent, contemporary verse:

**Stanza I**
Flee from the crowd, and cleave to constancy,
Let your own lot suffice, however small;
For hoarding breeds hate, and climbing, instability,
The throng breeds envy, and success blinds all.
Desire no more than need shall ever call;
Govern yourself well, you who counsel others' deeds,
And truth shall set thee free — of this, no fear.

**Stanza II**
Strive not to mend what fate has bent awry,
Trusting in her who spins as spins a ball;
Great peace may rest in modest industry —
Beware, then, lest against a goad you fall;
Contend not like the crock against the wall.
Master yourself, who master others' deeds,
And truth shall set thee free — of this, no fear.

**Stanza III**
What is bestowed on thee, take humbly, meek;
The wrestling for this world but ends in fall.
No home is here, but wilderness we seek —
Go forth, O pilgrim! Forth, O beast, from stall!
Know thine own country, look up, thank God for all!
Keep to the highest road, let spirit lead,
And truth shall set thee free — of this, no fear.

**Envoy**
Therefore, thou Vache, forsake thine old distress;
No longer to the world remain a thrall.
Cry out for mercy — He whose goodness blessed
Thee out of nothing, and, in special call,
Draw near to Him, and pray for one and all,
For thee and others, heaven's promised meed,
And truth shall set thee free — of this, no fear.

---

**Note:** I preserved the rhyme-royal form (ababbcc), the refrain, the address to "Vache," and every core image (the crock against the wall, Fortune's wheel, the pilgrim and beast, the wrestling match) while modernizing archaic vocabulary and syntax for greater clarity and flow. If you'd prefer a version that retains more of the original Middle English flavor, or a prose paraphrase instead, I'm happy to provide that as well.

# On the Vanity of Worldly Striving and the Pursuit of Truth

Flee from the pressing crowds of worldly life, and take up your dwelling in truthfulness instead. Learn to be content with what you possess, however small or humble it may seem, for the hoarding of goods breeds only envy and hatred among men, while ambition—the restless hunger for more—brings nothing but instability and unrest to the soul. The man who chases after every gain finds himself forever chasing shadows, never arriving at peace.

Do not exhaust yourself trying to straighten all that is crooked in this fickle, ever-turning world. The world spins on its wheel of fortune, indifferent to our efforts to correct it, and much sorrow comes to those who war against the tide of fate. Instead, turn your labor inward: govern yourself well, master your own passions and disorders, and you will find that a little effort spent rightly accomplishes more good than a lifetime spent battling forces beyond your control. Wisdom lies not in correcting the world, but in correcting oneself.

Accept with humility whatever portion is given to you, whether abundance or want, honor or obscurity. Remember always that this world is not your true home—it is but a wilderness, a place of exile through which you must pass as a pilgrim, seeking a homeland that lies elsewhere. Do not mistake the road for the destination, nor cling to the inn as though it were your house.

Therefore, look upward. Know that your true homeland is heaven, and let this knowledge orient every step you take. Give thanks to God for all things—the bitter as well as the sweet—for both serve His purposes. Let your spirit, not your flesh, be your guide, leading you along the higher path rather than keeping you enslaved to the anxious cares and vanities of worldly life. The soul that looks toward heaven walks more lightly upon the earth.

Finally, abandon the old wretchedness that has weighed upon you—the guilt, the fear, the attachment to lesser things—and turn wholly to God. Offer Him prayer and gratitude, for He has fashioned you out of His goodness and sustains you still. Seek truth above all else, for truth alone has the power to set you free. In this, let there be no doubt: the path of truth is the path of liberty, and whoever walks it faithfully shall not be abandoned.

# Chaucer's "Truth" (Balade de Bon Conseil): An Expansion

Geoffrey Chaucer's short but profound poem "Truth," also known by its fuller title "Balade de Bon Conseil" (Ballad of Good Counsel), stands as one of the most enduring pieces of moral wisdom literature from the Middle English period. Though brief in form—structured as a ballade with a recurring refrain—the poem carries a weight of philosophical and spiritual gravity that has resonated with readers for over six centuries.

## The Central Problem: Worldly Instability

At its core, the poem grapples with a fundamental human anxiety: the seductive but ultimately illusory promises of worldly success, wealth, and status. Chaucer, writing in an age of political intrigue and social upheaval, recognized that the pursuit of material gain and public recognition often leads not to fulfillment but to a kind of spiritual bondage. The world, he suggests, is inherently unstable—a place of "climbing tickleness" where fortune's wheel turns unpredictably, casting down the proud and elevating the humble in cycles that no one can control or predict.

## The Poet's Counsel: A Fourfold Path

In response to this instability, Chaucer offers his readers—addressed intimately as if a wise friend speaking to another—a series of practical and spiritual injunctions:

**Flee from the crowd (the "press"):** The poem advises withdrawal from the throng of ambitious society, the crowded marketplace of human striving where people compete, envy, and destroy one another in pursuit of transient rewards. This is not a call to complete isolation, but rather a warning against losing oneself in the crowd's values and priorities.

**Dwell with soothfastness (truth):** Rather than chasing external validation, the poem urges the cultivation of inner truthfulness—an integrity of character that remains constant regardless of external circumstances. This truth is both a moral quality and, in the medieval Christian sense, connected to divine and eternal reality.

**Let your possessions suffice, though they be small:** Chaucer counsels contentment with modest means, recognizing that the endless accumulation of wealth only breeds anxiety, envy, and moral corruption. Sufficiency, not abundance, is the key to peace.

**Master thyself:** Perhaps the most crucial piece of advice is the call to self-governance—to rule one's own passions, desires, and impulses rather than being ruled by them. This Stoic-influenced wisdom suggests that true freedom comes not from controlling external circumstances but from mastering one's internal responses to them.

## Accepting Fate with Humility

The poem also emphasizes a posture of humble acceptance toward one's circumstances. Rather than railing against fate or constantly striving to change one's station through worldly ambition, the speaker advises embracing what has been allotted, trusting that this acceptance itself is a form of wisdom. This is not passive resignation but an active spiritual discipline—a recognition that peace comes from aligning oneself with reality rather than constantly fighting against it.

## The World as Wilderness, Not Home

One of the poem's most striking images is its characterization of earthly existence as a "wilderness"—a temporary and unstable dwelling place rather than a permanent home. This metaphor draws on medieval Christian theology, which viewed earthly life as a pilgrimage toward a heavenly destination. By reminding readers that this world is not their true home, Chaucer relativizes worldly concerns and ambitions, placing them in proper perspective against eternal verities.

## The Refrain: Truth Shall Deliver

The poem's refrain—"And trouthe shall delivere, it is no drede" (and truth shall deliver you, there is no doubt)—serves as both consolation and imperative. This line encapsulates the poem's central thesis: that genuine liberation comes not from wealth, status, or worldly power, but from inner truth and moral integrity. This "truth" operates on multiple levels—as personal honesty, as fidelity to one's authentic self, and as alignment with divine truth.

## Conclusion: A Timeless Call to Integrity

Ultimately, "Truth" functions as a compact but comprehensive guide to spiritual and moral living in an uncertain world. Its message transcends its medieval context, speaking to universal human experiences of ambition, disappointment, and the search for meaning. By advocating for self-mastery, humble acceptance, contentment, and unwavering commitment to truth over material accumulation, Chaucer offers his readers a path toward genuine freedom—one that doesn't depend on controlling external circumstances but on cultivating an unshakeable inner integrity. In this way, the poem serves not merely as medieval moral instruction but as enduring wisdom literature that continues to speak meaningfully to readers navigating their own relationships with ambition, materialism, and the search for authentic fulfillment.

# On Sufficiency, Flexibility, and Purpose

There is a quiet wisdom in learning what is enough. In a world that constantly pushes us toward more—more achievement, more possessions, more validation—the ability to recognize sufficiency becomes almost a radical act. To say "this suffices" is not to settle for less, but to understand precisely what is needed and to stop there, freeing energy for what truly matters.

Flexibility plays a crucial role in this understanding. Rigid definitions of "enough" rarely survive contact with real life. What suffices in one season may fall short in another; what once felt essential may later reveal itself as excess. A flexible mind adjusts these boundaries as circumstances shift, neither clinging to arbitrary standards nor drifting endlessly in search of an ever-receding ideal. Flexibility, then, is not the absence of standards but the capacity to hold them loosely enough to respond to reality as it actually is.

But sufficiency and flexibility only make sense in light of purpose—the "for" that gives them direction. Enough, without knowing what it is enough *for*, becomes meaningless. A modest income might suffice for a life devoted to creative work, but not for one oriented toward ambitious travel. A single skill might suffice for a specific task, yet prove inadequate for a broader calling. The question "sufficient for what?" forces us to clarify our aims before we can meaningfully judge whether we have arrived at "enough."

Together, these three ideas form a kind of practical philosophy. Purpose gives us a reason to evaluate what we have. Flexibility allows us to reassess that evaluation as life changes. And sufficiency, once recognized, grants permission to stop striving and start living. Rather than measuring ourselves against infinite external standards, we learn to ask simpler, more honest questions: What is this for? Does it suffice? And can I remain open enough to notice when the answer changes?

In this way, contentment is not a fixed destination but an ongoing, adaptable practice—one that requires both clarity of purpose and the humility to keep adjusting our sense of what is truly enough.
